data.description:
## Summary

`docs/exit-codes.md` declares itself (`:5-6`) "the single source of truth for ... which
code each subcommand emits", and states (`:7-15`) that
`tests/interfaces/lifecycle/test_exit_codes.py` "cross-checks this file's per-command
table against the route registry, so a route with no row here ... fails the build."

That guarantee holds only for **top-level** routes. It does not hold for nested
subcommands, which is where most of the table's rows live.

## Evidence

`_live_route_names()` (`test_exit_codes.py:247-249`) builds
`{route.name for route in ROUTES if not route.retired}`. Measured on the live registry:

    'store' in live          -> True
    'store build-vectors'... -> 'build-vectors' in live -> False
    'footprint' in live      -> False
    len(live)                -> 53

The parity test's own docstring (`:254`) is accurate and says so plainly: "each table
row begins with a live top-level route. Nested invocations share that route." The
`orphaned` check keys on `row.split()[0]`, so a row for any `store <member>` is
accepted because `store` is live, and the `undocumented` check can never demand a row
for a member because no member name is in `live`.

Net effect: a new nested subcommand can land with no row, and nothing fails. Observed
directly — `rebar store build-vectors` (ticket 0461-09ce-4850-42a7) passed `make verify`
twice with no row in the table. The gap was caught by an LLM code-review advisory, not
by the build.

The table nonetheless carries a row for every other `store` member (`compact`, `fsck`,
`fsck-recover`, `maintenance`, `footprint`, `doctor`, `export`, `import` at `:159-202`),
so the convention is real and maintained by hand while the doc describes it as enforced.

## Why this matters beyond one missing row

This is the same defect class the file already documents about itself at `:12-15`:
"Until 2026-09 this file claimed a stronger guarantee than any test made, and the table
had drifted in both directions while carrying that claim." That correction narrowed the
claim on the *exit-value* axis (those columns are hand-authored) but left the
*row-coverage* claim unqualified, and on the nesting axis it is still too strong.

A doc that overstates its own enforcement is worse than one that states none: a reader
who trusts `:7-15` has no reason to check the table by hand, which is exactly how the
`build-vectors` row came to be missing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `docs/exit-codes.md` no longer claims a guarantee the parity test does not make:
      the row-coverage sentence states that enforcement covers top-level routes and
      that nested-subcommand rows are maintained by convention -- OR the parity test is
      extended so the claim becomes true.
- [ ] If the enforcement route is taken, a test fails when a live nested subcommand has
      no row, demonstrated by a mutation (remove one existing member row; the test
      must fail) and by the inverse (an invented member row names a real nested
      invocation or the test fails).
- [ ] If the documentation route is taken, the narrowed wording is shown to be accurate
      against `_live_route_names()` as measured, not asserted.
- [ ] `make verify` passes.

## Out of scope

The missing `store build-vectors` row itself -- that is fixed in 0461-09ce-4850-42a7's
own change, which is where the omission arose.
data.title: exit-codes.md claims a route-row guarantee the parity test does not make for nested subcommands
